title: Two Water Pipes on the Same Street
dek: In 1854 the mains of two south London water companies ran side by side into the same houses, so that two doors apart, the water people drank might be entirely different. John Snow decided to use this experiment nobody had designed to test a theory he had been arguing for five years.

sections.heading: An experiment nobody designed, and somebody recorded

paras.t: When cholera struck south London again in 1854, John Snow saw both a disaster and an opportunity he had long been waiting for. He had spent five years arguing that cholera spread through water, and for five years he had lacked a clinching piece of evidence. His resolve, as he wrote it down, was blunt: he would spare no exertion to ascertain the exact effect of the water supply on the progress of the epidemic, and he would do the work himself, so that the truth or fallacy of the doctrine would be settled in one decisive test.

The difficulty was to prise water apart from air, neighborhood and poverty — the sorts of thing people blamed and nobody could measure. South London happened to hand him a ready-made comparison. The pipes of each company went down all the streets, and into nearly all the courts and alleys; a few houses were supplied by one company and a few by the other, according to the decision of the owner or occupier at that time. Two households sharing a doorstep might be drinking entirely different water.

The story starts in 1852. That year the Lambeth Waterworks Company moved its works to Thames Ditton and began drawing from the river above London, thereby obtaining a supply of water quite free from the sewage of London. The other supplier in the area, the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, still drew its water from the tideway below the city. Where the two supplies overlapped, the mains of both companies ran down every street together.

Snow called this an experiment, and one on the grandest scale. "No fewer than three hundred thousand people of both Sexes, of every age and occupation, and of every rank and station, from gentlefolks down to the very poor, were divided into two groups without their choice, and, in most cases, without their knowledge" — one group drinking water mixed with the sewage of London, and with it whatever might have come from cholera patients, the other drinking water free of such impurity.

The author infers that this arrangement appealed to Snow precisely because both groups lived in one city, weathered one epidemic, breathed the same air and walked the same streets, so that the largest stable difference left standing was the water. That is the author's reading, however. Snow himself said only that he chose these places because "all the circumstances were so happily adapted for the inquiry".

sections.heading: Seven weeks of checking the water

paras.t: Cholera returned in 1854, and Snow did not wait for official statistics. In his own words, "I resolved to spare no exertion which might be necessary to ascertain the exact effect of the water supply on the progress of the epidemic", and he wanted to conduct the inquiry himself in order to obtain "the most satisfactory proof of the truth or fallacy of the doctrine which I had been advocating for five years." This was a test he staked his standing on, not routine registration.

The inquiry covered the streets where the two supplies were interleaved. Each company's mains ran down all the streets and into nearly all the courts and alleys; some houses took one company's water and some the other's, according to the decision of the owner or occupier at that time. That phrase — at that time — carries the point. The grouping was not invented once the epidemic began; it had been settled years earlier in deeds, water rates and plumbing, then largely forgotten.

In Snow's telling, the experiment stood unmatched in scale. No fewer than three hundred thousand people of every sex, age, occupation and rank — from gentlefolks down to the very poor — fell into one of two groups without their choice and, in most cases, without their knowledge: one group drinking water containing the sewage of London, the other drinking water free of such impurity. This was the cleanest comparison he could imagine, because neither group knew it was being compared.

The trouble was classification. Very few households could name their water company on the spot; even residents who paid the water rates themselves usually had to dig out a receipt before the name came back to them. Among working people who paid weekly rents, the rates were invariably paid by the landlord or his agent, often living at a distance, and the residents knew nothing about the matter. In other words, the poorest — least able to survive cholera — were exactly those least able to say which stretch of river their water came from.

Snow filled the gaps in memory with chemistry. "The test I employed was founded on the great difference in the quantity of chloride of sodium contained in the two kinds of water" — common salt, in plain terms. Measuring it let him identify a house's supplier without depending on the occupant's recollection. The method was homespun, but on the streets of 1854 it beat writing round to landlords.

The results of the first seven weeks went into a single table. Per ten thousand houses, deaths from cholera ran at 315 in the population supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company, 37 among Lambeth Company customers, and 59 in the rest of London. Snow's verdict: "The mortality in the houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company was therefore between eight and nine times as great as in the houses supplied by the Lambeth Company". Set the three numbers side by side and the gap needs no statistics to be seen.

The author infers that the comparison bites not only because 315 dwarfs 37, but because the rest of London's 59 lands squarely between them: one city, one epidemic, and the group whose only difference was its water dying at several times the rate. If the neighborhood or the air were doing the killing, the two groups should not have split so far apart. That layer of reasoning is the author's addition; Snow's own argument turned on the correspondence between water quality and death rates.

sections.heading: The parallel run is itself evidence

paras.t: The design earns its force from parallelism: two sets of pipes running like parallel lines across nearly identical populations, with nothing altered for the sake of an experiment. Whichever company a householder had picked was mostly a shrug at the moment of signing up. By 1854 that long-forgotten whim had become the largest difference between the two groups. One reading is that precisely because nobody arranged the split, the result is hard to spoil with anyone's wish to prove something.

The author sketches a counterfactual — an alternative design, not history. Had Snow compared London's average death rate, or a rich district against a poor one, wealth, housing and occupation would have crowded in and diluted the effect of water. The street-by-street pattern of two supplies running down the same road pressed those extraneous factors to a minimum. Snow was not waiting for more perfect data; he was waiting for a comparison that already existed, and what remained was to dig it out and check it.

Fictional modern scene one. A company finds two customer-service teams handling the same week's calls with different scripts, a leftover of a system migration. Nobody designed an experiment, and nobody wants to wait six months before rolling out a new process. So the team lead pulls the same class of tickets from both groups and compares: the same kinds of questions, and one group's callback rate is far lower. He need not prove that this script wins in every situation; he only has to decide which one to roll out this week.

Fictional modern scene two. In an apartment block, two internet providers ran cabling at the same time, and tenants picked one almost at random when signing the lease. Six months on, residents complain that video calls keep dropping. The property manager sends no questionnaire round the flats; he simply maps which households log the faults and checks which provider's line they are on. Same building, same lifts, same rain — and the only difference left is the wire.

Plainly: every figure and every account in this piece comes from Snow's own book and his own tables, with no independent check by a health authority or any third party at the time. When the same man proposes the doctrine, conducts the inquiry and compiles the statistics, that does not make the data wrong — but it does mean we are reading one side's record.

Second, the ready-made experiment is Snow's own argumentative framing, not strict randomization. The owner's or occupier's choice of company was no lottery draw, and may have tracked rent levels, the age of the house or the address (that link is the author's speculation; the record notes only that the decision rested with the owner or occupier, and that for weekly tenants the rates were paid by a landlord or agent living at a distance). Treating the two groups as comparable rests on the approximation of the same street and the same epidemic, not on randomization itself.

Finally, this piece works from OCR text of a scanned copy, and some figures in the original are already garbled nearby. Only three legible numbers from the table are used here — 315, 37 and 59 — together with the conclusion of "between eight and nine times". No other ratios or breakdowns are cited.

reflection.scenario: You own a process that happens to be running in two versions at once. Because of legacy arrangements from a system migration, some customers go through version A and some through version B. The two groups broadly resemble each other, but the split was not random. Next quarter you must settle on one standard way of working — and your data is only a few weeks old.
reflection.question: When the evidence is still incomplete, what would make you change course? Would you wait until the gap is too large to argue away, or act once the difference is stark enough and the rival explanations can be held down? Which mistake frightens you more — being too early, or being too late?

assumptions: The two customer groups broadly resemble each other, but the split was not random; unseen differences (customer type, account manager) may exist.
Only a few weeks of data; the sample is not large, but both groups left complete records.
Changing the process has a cost; so does not changing it.
No perfect experiment is coming; you can only judge on the comparison in front of you.
steps: Write down first where the differences between the two groups could come from: besides the process itself, what else could explain the gap in results?
Pick the most dangerous rival explanation and find one piece of evidence that pins it down — a comparison within the same class of customer, the equivalent of Snow's single street.
Compare only data you are confident in; skip suspect breakdowns, and turn the gap into plain language (one runs at several times the rate of the other) before reaching for a complicated model.
Set a line for action: how large the gap must be and how well the rival explanations must be pinned down before you switch. Below the line, keep watching — and write down the date to look again.
example.alternative: The author's other option: keep both versions running for now, treat the split as an ongoing comparison, and decide when the data has run longer. The cost is that one group of customers goes on using the weaker process in the meantime; the benefit is avoiding a wholesale change made on incomplete data. Which way you go depends on which error you mind more.

uncertainty_note: Every figure, account and first-person statement in this piece comes from the relevant passages and tables of the second edition (1855) of John Snow's On the Mode of Communication of Cholera; no independent verification by a health authority or anyone else at the time has been found. The phrases "natural experiment" and "ready-made experiment" are Snow's own argumentative wording; the owner's or occupier's choice of a water company was not strict randomization. This piece uses OCR text and adopts only the three clear figures from the table (315, 37, 59) and the conclusion of eight to nine times the mortality; no other values from garbled OCR are cited, and nothing is drawn on later assessments or the subsequent development of bacteriology.
